name: Inpass
subcategory: corporate wellness benefit / gym network access
tagline: A corporate wellbeing benefit platform that gives employees access to a network of gyms, studios and wellness providers through one membership.

pricing.notes: AI-drafted from a site submission; price unverified. B2B wellness benefit platforms typically quote per employee and do not publish rates.

verdictSummary: The software here is the least interesting part: a check-in screen, a membership record, a provider directory, some usage reporting. The actual product is a signed roster of gyms and studios that agreed to accept your pass and get paid for it, plus the HR contract on the other side that pays for it. You can clone the app in an afternoon and it will be worth nothing, because no gym front desk has any reason to recognize your QR code. There is also the unglamorous middle layer: reconciling visits into payouts, handling per-visit caps and fraud, and whatever local labor and tax treatment applies to a wellbeing benefit. The closest honest personal build is a tracker for the gym memberships and classes you already pay for yourself.
coreLoopDIY: A local app that logs your workouts and class visits across the gyms you personally pay for, tracks cost per visit, and tells you which membership you are wasting money on.
requirements: Local machine or a small VPS to run it on
Your own memberships, since no gym network comes with this
whatYouLose: The gym and studio network itself, which is the entire product
Employer funding, since the benefit only exists because a company pays for it
Reciprocal access: your QR code opens no doors
Visit reconciliation and payouts between the platform and each provider
HR-side reporting, eligibility rules and whatever compliance the benefit carries locally
moatNotes: Two-sided: employers on one side, hundreds of independent gyms on the other. Neither side joins for the software.
whyPeopleStillPay: Companies buy this because negotiating with forty gyms individually is a nightmare and employees want variety without forty memberships. Employees use it because it is free to them and the card works at the place near the office and the place near home. None of that value is code. It is a sales team that spent years signing providers, a billing system that pays those providers correctly every month, and an HR contract that makes it a line item instead of an expense claim. A personal clone has zero of those and cannot bootstrap them.
notes: The check-in app is a one-sitting build; the gym roster is not. The moat is a two-sided network of signed providers and employer contracts, held together by monthly reconciliation nobody wants to rebuild.
prompt:
Build a local-first personal fitness membership tracker called "PassLog". This is a consolation build: it does NOT give access to any gym network, it tracks the memberships you already pay for yourself.

Stack, no substitutions:
- Next.js 15 App Router, TypeScript, Tailwind.
- SQLite via better-sqlite3, file at ./data/passlog.db.
- No auth, no accounts, no cloud, no telemetry. Single user on localhost.

Data model:
- providers: id, name, type (gym | studio | pool | other), address, notes.
- memberships: id, provider_id, plan_name, monthly_cost, currency, started_on, ended_on nullable, visit_cap_per_month nullable.
- visits: id, provider_id, visited_on, activity, duration_minutes, rating 1 to 5 nullable, note.

Features that must work:
- Add, edit, archive providers and memberships.
- Log a visit in under five seconds: pick provider, date defaults to today, optional activity and duration, save.
- Dashboard: current month visits per provider, cost per visit for each active membership (monthly_cost divided by visits this month), and a plain-language flag when cost per visit exceeds a configurable threshold or when visits for the month are zero.
- Calendar heatmap of visits for the trailing twelve months.
- A "should I cancel this" table ranking active memberships by trailing three month cost per visit.
- CSV export of visits and a CSV import that accepts the same shape.

Explicitly out of scope: QR codes, check-in validation, provider payouts, employer billing, multi-user roles, mobile app, push notifications, any external API.

Seed the database with three example providers and about forty visits across the last ninety days so the dashboard is not empty on first run.

Ship a README with setup in four commands or fewer. Put any config in .env.example, including THRESHOLD_COST_PER_VISIT and DEFAULT_CURRENCY. Commit nothing to .env.
